notes: Complete Court of Appeal judgment on preliminary passing-off/trade mark issue.

enrichment.short_title: Passing-off goodwill date preserved despite retrospective trade mark registration under Trade Marks Act 1994
key_facts: Inter Lotto operated pub lotteries using the name HOTPICK from mid-2001; Camelot applied on 17 October 2001 to register HOTPICKS and launched Lotto Hotpicks in July 2002.
Inter Lotto sued for trade mark infringement and passing off, alleging confusion between the games.
Patten J ordered a preliminary issue on whether 17 October 2001 was the date for assessing Inter Lotto's passing-off goodwill.
Camelot argued that post-application use by Inter Lotto was prospectively unlawful once registration took retrospective effect, so later goodwill could not count.
The judge rejected Camelot's broader 'guillotine' and ex turpi causa arguments but the Court of Appeal reached the same outcome on different reasoning.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from a preliminary issue in trade mark infringement and passing-off proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; leave to appeal refused; Camelot to pay Inter Lotto's costs.
enrichment.ratio: Section 2(2) of the Trade Marks Act 1994 expressly preserves the law of passing off, so a registered trade mark's retrospective effect from the application date cannot be used to exclude reputation and goodwill built up after that date but before the defendant's market use; the relevant date for passing off remains when the defendant goes to market, not the date of the trade mark application.
legal_issues: Whether the date of a trade mark application fixes the date for assessing passing-off goodwill
Whether post-application use alleged to infringe a subsequently registered mark can be ignored in passing off
Whether section 2(2) preserves passing off notwithstanding sections 5(4), 9 and 40
Whether ex turpi causa or illegality principles apply to trade mark infringement before registration

notes: Complete Court of Appeal judgment refusing permission for judicial review of FSA warning notices.

enrichment.short_title: FSA could lawfully use section 56 prohibition procedure after section 66 misconduct time bar expired
key_facts: Former Brandeis (Brokers) Limited employees faced SFA misconduct proceedings over LME customer complaints from 1997-1998.
The SFA proceedings were discontinued when FSMA 2000 replaced the 1986 Act and the two-year section 66(4) time limit had expired.
In June 2002 the FSA issued section 57 warning notices proposing section 56 prohibition orders on fitness and propriety grounds.
The applicants sought judicial review, arguing the FSA was circumventing the expired disciplinary route under section 66.
Lightman J refused permission; Laws LJ granted permission to appeal that refusal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against refusal of permission to apply for judicial review of FSA warning notices.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; permission for judicial review refused; applicants to pay the FSA's costs.
enrichment.ratio: Section 56 prohibition powers are regulatory and forward-looking but may properly be used in respect of past misconduct where a person is not fit and proper; they are not barred because section 66 disciplinary action is time-barred, and judicial review is an inappropriate route where the statutory tribunal procedure provides the proper remedy.
legal_issues: Whether use of section 56 after expiry of the section 66(4) time limit is an abuse of process
Whether prohibition and disciplinary powers are sharply divided as punitive versus preventive
Whether future intention to work in regulated activity is required before a warning notice
Whether judicial review should be refused for alternative remedy and prematurity

notes: Complete Court of Appeal judgment on Article 7 and post-release licence under the Criminal Justice Act 1991.

enrichment.short_title: Post-1991 Act release on licence is a heavier Article 7 penalty for pre-Act offenders
key_facts: Mr Uttley committed serious sexual offences before the 1991 Act came into force but was sentenced in 1995 to 12 years' imprisonment.
Under the 1991 Act he would be released at two-thirds but remain on licence until three-quarters, with recall and further-offence consequences.
Before 1991, standard remission meant unconditional release at two-thirds with no licence period.
Moses J dismissed the claim that the licence regime breached Article 7 ECHR.
The Court of Appeal held the licence period was an integral part of the sentence and more onerous than the pre-1991 position.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from Administrative Court refusal of declarations of incompatibility under the Human Rights Act 1998.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; declaration of incompatibility made under section 4(2) HRA 1998; leave to appeal to the House of Lords refused.
enrichment.ratio: For Article 7 purposes the statutory licence period following release is part of the penalty imposed on conviction, not merely execution of sentence; where an offender committed offences before the 1991 Act but was sentenced under it, mandatory release on licence with conditions, recall and further-sentence exposure is a heavier penalty than unconditional release at two-thirds under the former remission system.
legal_issues: Whether licence conditions and recall under section 33 constitute a penalty under Article 7(1) ECHR
Whether licence provisions are part of the sentence or separate post-conviction measures
Whether transitional provisions in Schedule 12 to the 1991 Act are compatible with Article 7
Whether the relevant date is offence, conviction or sentence

enrichment.short_title: Mareva inquiry damages upheld after valuing subcontractor including associated invoicing company profits
key_facts: Johnson sub-contracted electrical work at a Glaxo Stevenage project to Techni-Track Europa Ltd (Europa) in 1993-1994.
Johnson obtained a freezing order in February 1994, Europa was locked out, and the bank called in debts leading to administrative receivership.
The Mareva injunction was set aside on 23 February 1994 with an inquiry as to damages, later consolidated with contract claims.
The judge valued Europa at £225,000 for maintainable earnings and awarded £64,000 for unpaid contractual work.
Johnson appealed valuation methodology, contractual classification and costs; Europa cross-appealed on annualisation of earnings.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal and cross-appeal from Technology and Construction Court judgment on Mareva inquiry damages and counterclaim.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed only to remove £1,847 unclaimed bank interest; all other grounds of appeal and the cross-appeal dismissed.
enrichment.ratio: In a Mareva damages inquiry a prudent purchaser may look to economic reality rather than strict corporate form, so profits routed through associated invoicing company Engineering could be included in Europa's valuation; disputed unagreed claims excluded from maintainable earnings on one side of the account did not preclude neutralising their cost impact where the judge accepted expert evidence they were a one-off distortion.
legal_issues: Whether associated company profits could be included in the valuation of Europa
Whether disallowed counterclaim sums should be excluded from maintainable earnings
Whether the judge erred in treating post-January work as contractual debt rather than damages
Whether the judge should have annualised maintainable earnings in the cross-appeal

enrichment.short_title: Fault-tolerant disk-array patent claims 1 and 2 held obvious over acknowledged prior art
key_facts: Storage Computer Corporation owned European patent EP 0294287 for a fault-tolerant error-correcting storage system using parallel disk drives and a dedicated error/recovery disk.
Pumfrey J held claims 1 and 2 invalid for obviousness and not infringed by Hitachi.
Storage appealed after a settlement under which Hitachi took no part in the appeal.
The pre-characterising features of claim 1 were acknowledged as old, including disclosure in Timsit; the dispute concerned the characterising cache and intelligence features.
The Court of Appeal upheld obviousness applying the Windsurfing test and Professor Katz's evidence on IBM 1 concepts.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from Chancery Division patent infringement and validity trial; respondent absent after settlement.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed on validity; no order as to costs.
enrichment.ratio: Where the pre-characterising portion of a disk-array patent claim was acknowledged as disclosed in prior art such as Timsit, adding common general knowledge cache and scheduling concepts from IBM 1 to achieve asynchronous buffered read/write with intelligent allocation was an obvious step requiring no inventive step under section 3 of the Patents Act 1977.
legal_issues: Whether claims 1 and 2 were obvious over Timsit and common general knowledge
Whether an admission in the patent could substitute for direct prior art analysis
Whether IBM 1 concepts were common general knowledge
Whether the appeal could properly proceed without adversarial argument from Hitachi

notes: Complete Commercial Court judgment on charterparty arrest and repudiatory redelivery.

enrichment.short_title: Charterers' arrest did not suspend hire under clause 60; award remitted on White and Carter damages
key_facts: Owners chartered The Dynamic to Koch Carbon on an amended NYPE form for a cement/clinker voyage ending at Myrtle Grove in August 1999.
Charterers arrested the vessel on 2 August 1999 for security; discharge completed on 3 August and the vessel remained under arrest until 17 August.
Owners claimed hire continued during arrest; Charterers said redelivery occurred after discharge.
The arbitrator held clause 60 did not put the vessel off hire where Charterers caused the arrest, found repudiatory redelivery, but denied hire damages because no loss was shown.
Morison J largely upheld the arbitrator but remitted issues on White and Carter and damages calculation.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal under section 69 of the Arbitration Act 1996 against interim final LMAA arbitration award.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed on clause 60 construction and repudiation issues; award remitted for reconsideration of White and Carter and damages for the arrest period.
enrichment.ratio: Clause 60 of the NYPE charterparty was not intended to suspend hire where charterers themselves arrested the vessel during the charter; where owners did not accept repudiation, whether they were bound to do so and the measure of damages depend on White and Carter principles and require loss to be assessed by reference to contractual hire until proper redelivery, not by attributing later voyage earnings to the arrest period.
legal_issues: Construction of clause 60 where charterers arrest the vessel
Whether purported redelivery after discharge was repudiatory
Whether owners were bound to accept repudiation under White and Carter
Whether damages could equal unpaid hire for the arrest period

enrichment.short_title: Duty of care in unfounded child abuse investigations owed to child but not parents after Human Rights Act
key_facts: Three conjoined appeals involved unfounded child abuse allegations by health and social care professionals against parents, causing psychiatric harm and temporary separation.

East Berks concerned a false Munchausen syndrome by proxy accusation; Dewsbury a misdiagnosed sexual abuse allegation; Oldham a non-accidental injury finding later explained by osteogenesis imperfecta.
Preliminary issues asked whether a Caparo duty of care existed and whether Article 6 ECHR was violated by striking out claims.
The Court held Bedfordshire no longer barred a duty to the child after the Human Rights Act, but parents still had no duty where interests conflicted with the child.
Dewsbury child's claim against the local authority was allowed to proceed; parent claims and the other appeals were dismissed.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Conjoined appeals from strike-out/preliminary issue decisions in negligence claims arising from child protection investigations.
enrichment.outcome: Dewsbury child's appeal allowed against the local authority; Dewsbury father's, East Berks and Oldham appeals dismissed; leave to the House of Lords refused.
enrichment.ratio: Striking out unfounded child abuse negligence claims for lack of duty does not violate Article 6; post-Human Rights Act a common law duty of care may be owed to a child in child protection investigations but not to parents where their interests conflict with the child's, and witness immunity does not automatically shield investigative social work following Darker v Chief Constable of the West Midlands Police.
legal_issues: Whether X v Bedfordshire still precludes negligence claims by parents and children
Whether Article 6 requires full trial before duty is ruled out
Whether Article 8 requires a different negligence test
Whether witness immunity applies to child protection investigations
Whether Caparo proximity is satisfied for parent claimants

notes: Interim meaning and strike-out ruling in libel claim; final trial issues remain.

enrichment.short_title: Libel meanings in Stephen Lawrence book partly struck out but safety and racism allegations remain
key_facts: Claimant Elvin Oduro, a childhood friend of Stephen Lawrence, sued over Duwayne Brooks's book 'Steve and Me' published by Time-Life Entertainment Group.
The book portrayed Oduro as a peripheral acquaintance who failed to protect Stephen, exaggerated their friendship, threatened Brooks at the Old Bailey, and expressed racist hostility to white people.
The defendant applied to strike out meanings as not defamatory or not capable of being borne.
Tugendhat J ruled on natural and ordinary meaning and strike-out under CPR Part 53.
Several pleaded meanings survived for trial, including putting Stephen in danger, aggression at court, racism, and exaggerating closeness to Stephen.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court ruling on meaning and strike-out application in libel proceedings before trial.
enrichment.outcome: Partial strike-out: some meanings removed; meanings at paragraphs 7.1, 7.2, 7.3 (partial), 7.4, 7.5 and 8 (partial) remain for jury trial.
enrichment.ratio: A publication must be read as a whole by the fair-minded ordinary reasonable reader; passages separated by many pages cannot support an over-elaborate meaning about parental assessments of safety, and claims that a young man lied about being another's 'best friend' are too strong where exaggeration is the natural reading, but allegations of failing to protect Stephen, aggressive threats at court, racist remarks, and grossly exaggerating friendship closeness are capable of defamatory meaning and cannot be withdrawn from the jury.
legal_issues: Whether passages in the book are capable of bearing the pleaded defamatory meanings
Whether meanings should be withdrawn from the jury as perverse
Whether strike-out is appropriate where justification or fair comment may fail at trial
Whether innuendo meanings about lying and friendship closeness are sustainable

notes: Complete Family Division judgment on inherent jurisdiction over incapacitated adult.

enrichment.short_title: Incapacitated adult's best interests required local authority residential placement despite father's care
key_facts: S, aged 33, has moderate/severe learning disability, atypical autism and epilepsy and lacks capacity to decide residence or contact.
Her father Mr S had cared for her since her mother's death in 1995 with private support workers and day centre attendance.
After a disputed November 2002 incident during a flu vaccination visit, Newham removed S under inherent jurisdiction interim orders in December 2002.
Expert evidence from Dr C and independent social worker Mr O'M supported a specialist eight-bed local authority home opening in August 2003.
The court found several historical allegations against Mr S not proved but still held placement in local authority care was in S's best interests.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court inherent jurisdiction final hearing on declarations as to capacity, residence and contact for a mentally incapacitated adult.
enrichment.outcome: Declarations made that S lacks capacity and that residence in local authority arranged accommodation and regulated contact with her father are in her best interests.
enrichment.ratio: In inherent jurisdiction proceedings for incapacitated adults there is no Children Act threshold; once incapacity and a serious justiciable welfare issue are established, the court applies a Re A balance-sheet best-interests test and need not make adverse historical findings against a family carer if professional evidence shows future specialist placement better meets the adult's long-term needs, safeguards and family contact.
legal_issues: Whether the court has inherent jurisdiction where Mental Health Act guardianship criteria are not met
Whether unfounded historical abuse findings are necessary before overriding parental care
How Re A balance-sheet analysis applies to incapacitated adults
What contact and safeguarding arrangements should accompany declaratory relief
